articles.title: Startup eyed over flight chaos funnels cash to Transportation chief's son-in-law
articles.description: The developer of a new AI system now under scrutiny as airplanes stand grounded nationwide funneled cash into the political campaign of Transportation chief Sean Duffy's son-in-law, records show. Air Space Intelligence, the contractor Duffy announced in June would develop the Federal Aviation Administration's new AI-powered air traffic management system, contributed $12,500 to the congressional campaign of U.S. Rep.-elect Michael Alfonso (R-WI) in March this year, federal records show. The contract it won was worth up to $875.9 million. The Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) system launched this week, according to CNN National Security analyst Juliette Kayyem. "The FAA onboarded a new AI system 3 days ago," Kayyem wrote on X. "Hard to believe it's a coincidence." Air Space Intelligence's X account tweeted a denial that it was involved in Friday's chaotic downing of the national aviation system. "The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC," it wrote. One month after Duffy announced Air Space Intelligence's SMART would be used to cut delays and optimize airspace, Politico reported the Federal Aviation Administration was working to buy an ownership stake. It wasn't long before Congress members were raising the alarm about Air Space Intelligence and the system it was starting to unroll. "Concerningly, the nation’s frontline aviation safety workforce apparently had little to no input into SMART’s development and have received limited training and information during the current deployment process," 23 House representatives wrote last month. "The use of artificial intelligence within SMART has rightfully raised serious questions about its reliability and safety benefits."

articles.title: Trump superfan now 'done' with president: 'He's the king of the swamp'
articles.description: One of Donald Trump’s most avid — and visible — supporters has gone public with his split with the president after the midterm blowout that made the Republicans the minority party in Congress. Rick Frazier, 70, spent a decade as one of Trump’s “Front Row Joes,” the "superfans" who follow him to rallies across the country. His western Ohio home is still full of keepsakes, including a photo signed by Trump and a letter the president sent after Frazier’s daughter died of an overdose in 2023. The retired factory worker was won over in 2015, believing Trump would clean up Washington. Now he watches “South Park” mock the president and laughs along. “He’s the king of swamp,” Frazier told the Washington Post. Speaking with the Post, he admitted that his disillusionment built slowly. Frazier was frustrated by Trump’s reluctance to release the full Epstein files and by his rally-stage mockery of the word “affordability.” The breaking point was Trump’s pardon of a former Honduran president convicted of helping traffic cocaine into the U.S., a move Frazier couldn’t reconcile with the drug crisis that killed his daughter. “See, that got me all upset,” he told the Post adding he is "done" with Trump. In the midterms, he stuck with his Republican congressman, Jim Jordan (R-OH), but voted for Democrats for governor and Senate as Ohio flipped blue. Frazier says he’ll return to voting for the best candidate, regardless of party. He still likes Vice President JD Vance. But for now, he’s a voter up for grabs, telling the Post, “I’m kind of going to go back to the way I was before Trump, I was independently swinging wherever the best guy was running. And that’s the way I think it should be."

articles.title: Iraq: Mosul’s nine years of healing
articles.description: Mosul today is very different from the city the world saw during the battle. It is no longer a city in ruins,” says Suhaib Raad, a radio operator at Nablus hospital in Mosul, Iraq, which is currently supported by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF). He began working at the entrance to the emergency room when the facility opened in June 2017, one month before the battle officially ended. “In those early days, conditions were incredibly brutal,” says Suhaib. “The emergency room was constantly receiving casualties and patients of all backgrounds and ages, who needed treatment for severe illnesses and horrific war wounds.” A lifeline in a devastated city In October 2016, a nine-month military offensive to retake Mosul began after the city had spent nearly three years under the control of the Islamic State group. The fighting killed and injured thousands of people, displaced more than one million, and left large parts of Iraq’s second-largest city devastated. By the time the battle officially ended on 10 July 2017, much of Mosul's infrastructure, including its healthcare system, had been severely damaged. “The hospitals had been destroyed and there were no health services,” says Abdullah Isaa, an emergency nurse at Nablus hospital. “So, MSF opened this facility. People needed it. We treated many patients and saved many lives.” Initially operating as a field hospital, Nablus hospital received critical emergency cases from West Mosul, where the city's healthcare infrastructure had been destroyed or was otherwise no longer functioning. “In the immediate aftermath of the battle, MSF was the main healthcare provider in West Mosul,” explains Gemma Dominguez, MSF head of mission in Iraq. ��Over the years, the authorities have gradually rebuilt and rehabilitated some of the hospitals, allowing more health services to resume.” As Mosul slowly recovered, the main public hospitals began to reopen, at first operating from temporary structures and caravans. Yet the continued high number of patients admitted to Nablus highlighted the ongoing need for specialised care. From 2018 to 2022, MSF teams assisted with an increasing number of deliveries, reaching a peak of 1,000 deliveries per month, while providing inpatient care for adults and children with urgent medical needs. As other hospitals resumed services, the needs of the community evolved. In response, Nablus hospital adapted its activities, transitioning from a broad emergency response facility to a specialised paediatric emergency and maternity hospital, with a particular focus on emergency obstetric care and caesarean sections. Sabah Faisal Farhan, a data entry operator in the emergency ward, has witnessed the hospital's evolution firsthand. “The transformation has been remarkable,” she says. “We went from treating war injuries – which thank God have ended – to responding to the COVID-19 pandemic and caring for patients in quarantine. Once the pandemic was over, we refocused our care exclusively on children under the age of 14.” In total, teams at the hospital carried out more than 250,000 emergency consultations and more than 125,000 patients were admitted between 2017 and 2026. Expanding and innovating to improve the quality of care Supporting the hospital's growth and continued delivery of quality care has required constant adaptation and innovation from our medical and logistics teams. Over the years, they have developed and implemented solutions to improve the hospital's infrastructure, safety, and environmental management. These include a machine that turns infectious medical waste into non-hazardous waste by shredding and sterilising it, and a wastewater treatment system that uses specialised bacteria to decontaminate water before it is released into the drainage network. Another major success of this project is the mini-laboratory for bacterial testing, set up in 2022. It revealed high levels of antibiotic resistance among people. Over the years, MSF shared these findings with the health authorities, along with guidance on antibiotic stewardship and training in infection prevention and control. Mental health was also an important component of the hospital’s work. “The stories people share during psychological consultations have changed,” says Safa Abdulkareem Abd Al-Badrani, an MSF psychological counsellor. “Although the difficulties they describe are still connected in some way to the consequences of the war, they are now less about war-related trauma and more about losing a job or a loved one.” A place of birth and emotions Nablus hospital is a place where many people’s stories unfold. “We have been through a lot at this hospital, especially in the maternity department,” says Jellan Mohammed, the maternity supervisor. “At times, we would receive a critical case every week and we handled each one as a team. These cases showed the results of our efforts — when we saved a mother’s life, we were saving her baby’s life as well.” Sanad, now six-years-old, is one of the 88,000 children delivered in Nablus hospital over the past nine years. Like him, all his younger brothers and sisters were born at the hospital. “When my wife was discharged, she told me how well they had looked after her and the baby,” says Hadi Ali Ahmed Mohammad, Sanad’s father. “I thought to myself that anyone having a baby should come here.” This facility is where the family, who live in a village west of Mosul, seek paediatric care. “Once, my daughter got sick with a high fever, so I brought her here, and she stayed for a few days,” says Hadi Ali. “After that, she was much better, and went home happy.” Sanad and his father have come back to visit the family’s newborn, who is hospitalised in the neonatal unit. In the same ward is baby Zaid, who was born at the rebuilt Al-Batool hospital and referred to Nablus for jaundice. “He is a miracle baby,” says his mother. “We had been trying to have a baby for 10 years. Since he was born a few days ago, ithas felt like a dream. It’s very emotional. There’s a bit of worry, but mostly joy!” A city's journey towards healing “Mosul has undergone a complete transformation, a wonderful change for the better,” says Sabah. The bridges are busy with traffic, the markets are full again, and every corner of the old city is being rebuilt. Many relatives of patients say that, although finding work in Mosul is still very difficult, they recognise that the city is now safe and hope it stays that way. “We sincerely hope that the painful chapters are now behind us, and we look forward to seeing Mosul prosper for many years to come,” says Suhaib. “Today, people have access to healthcare services,” says Gemma. “Our collaboration with the Directorate of Health has played an important role in ensuring high-quality care, both at Nablus hospital and across the public health system.” “We are proud of what has been achieved here,” she says. “This is the right moment to hand over the hospital and build on these achievements, while continuing to respond to other critical healthcare needs in Iraq.” At the end of December, MSF will hand over Nablus hospital, which will continue operating as a public maternity hospital. As this chapter comes to a close, the hospital's legacy lives on in the hundreds of thousands of patients cared for and in the staff whose dedication and commitment shaped its journey. “Our lives have completely changed over these nine years. Mine, in particular, has changed profoundly,” says Sabah. “The services we provided will never be forgotten by the people of Mosul, and we will never forget the patients we saw and all the things we were able to help with.” MSF has worked in Iraq since 2003. As the country’s health system gradually recovers after decades of conflict and instability, MSF continues to address remaining gaps, particularly in women’s health. In Baghdad, MSF collaborates with the National Tuberculosis Institute to support the national tuberculosis programme by strengthening treatment protocols, training healthcare staff, ensuring a continuous supply of medicines, and conducting screening in places of detention. These activities aim to improve early detection, treatment adherence and the overall quality of tuberculosis care. MSF also supports the directorates of health in several governorates and the ministries of health in federal Iraq and the Kurdistan region through staff training, and improved mass casualty and emergency management. Our teams also provide emergency medical support and donations of medical supplies to healthcare facilities in times of need to ensure that access to quality healthcare services is not disrupted during emergencies.
